items.title: The Basic Structure of an HTML Element
items.text:
HTML pages are built from elements, small labelled chunks that tell the browser what each bit of content actually is, not just how it looks.

Say you write:

<p>Hello, world!</p>

That's a paragraph element. Nothing fancy, but if you get how it's put together, the rest of HTML clicks pretty quickly.

items.title: 1. The Basic Pattern
items.text:
Most elements follow this shape:

<element>Content</element>

So this:

<p>Hello, world!</p>

is really three pieces working together:

<p>        Hello, world!        </p>
 │               │                │
 │               │                └── Closing tag
 │               └────────────────── Content
 └────────────────────────────────── Opening tag

Put those three together and you've got an element.

items.title: 2. The Opening Tag
items.text:
This is where the browser learns "an element starts here."

<p>

If we pull it apart:

<   p   >
│   │   │
│   │   └── Closing angle bracket
│   └────── Element name
└────────── Opening angle bracket
An opening tag

The name in the middle is what matters, it says what kind of element you're opening. For instance:

<p>
that's a paragraph. 

<h1>
that's the main heading.

<strong>
that's strongly important text, not just "bold for looks".

items.title: 3. The Content
items.text:
This is simply what's inside the element.

<p>Hello, world!</p>

The content there is:

Hello, world!

Another one:

<h1>Learning HTML</h1>

Content:

Learning HTML

And content isn't always just plain text. You can tuck other elements inside too:

<p>
    This is <strong>very important</strong> information.
</p>

Here the paragraph holds both text and a <strong> element.

items.title: 4. The Closing Tag
items.text:
Same idea, but it says "we're done."

</p>

Spot the /? That's the giveaway.

Compare:

<p>

with:

</p>

That slash marks it as the closing tag:

<   p   >
│   │   │
│   │   └── Closing angle bracket
│   └────── Element name
└────────── Opening angle bracket

vs.

<   /   p   >
│   │   │   │
│   │   │   └── Closing angle bracket
│   │   └────── Element name
│   └────────── Forward slash
└────────────── Opening angle bracket
A closing tag

items.title: 5. The Complete Element
items.text:
When you combine the three, you get the full package:

<p>Hello, world!</p>

Broken down:

<p>          → Opening tag

Hello, world! → Content

</p>         → Closing tag

Or more simply:

Opening tag + Content + Closing tag = Element

items.title: 6. Another Example
items.text:
Take:

<h1>My Website</h1>

That gives us:

  • <h1>: opening tag
  • My Website: content
  • </h1>: closing tag
  • all of it together: an HTML element

One more, just to lock it in:

<strong>Important information</strong>

<strong>                 Opening tag
Important information    Content
</strong>                Closing tag

items.title: 7. Elements Can Contain Other Elements
items.text:
Elements can live inside other elements, we call it nesting.

<p>
    This is <strong>important</strong> information.
</p>

The <strong> sits inside the <p>. If you sketch it as a tree:

<p>
│
├── This is
│
├── <strong>
│   └── important
│
└── information.

That's how you build more interesting pages from simple pieces.

items.title: 8. Proper Nesting
items.text:
When you nest, close in the right order. Ever closed a box before putting the lid on inside?

This works:

<p>
    This is <strong>important</strong> information.
</p>

The <strong> opens and closes entirely inside <p>.

This doesn't:

<p>
    This is <strong>important</p> information</strong>

They're overlapping, browsers will try to guess what you meant, but don't make them.

A handy rule of thumb:

Last opened, first closed.

Like this:

<p>
    <strong>
        Important text
    </strong>
</p>

We opened <strong> last, so we close it first.

items.title: 9. Attributes
items.text:
Elements can carry attributes, extra info about that element.

<a href="https://example.com">Visit Example</a>

Start from a bare element:

<a>Visit Example</a>

Now add detail to its opening tag:

<a href="https://example.com">

Here:

<a
│
└── Element name

href
│
└── Attribute name

"https://example.com"
│
└── Attribute value
HTML attributes on the opening tag

In general:

<element attribute="value">
    Content
</element>

For instance:

<a href="https://example.com">
    Visit Example
</a>

items.title: 10. Multiple Attributes
items.text:
Yep, you can have more than one, just keep them inside the opening tag:

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A sleeping cat" width="400">

That one carries three:

src   → cat.jpg
alt   → A sleeping cat
width → 400

Pattern:

<element attribute="value" attribute="value">
    Content
</element>

items.title: 11. Not Every Element Has a Closing Tag
items.text:
Some elements don't wrap content at all, so they don't need a closer.

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A sleeping cat">

There's no </img>, it wouldn't make sense. We call it a void element.

You'll see a few others a lot:

<br>
<hr>
<input>
<meta>
<link>

No content between tags, just the element itself.

items.title: 12. Element vs Tag: Not Quite the Same
items.text:
Take:

<p>Hello</p>

The tags are:

<p>

and:

</p>

The element is the whole thing:

<p>Hello</p>

So simply:

A tag is a marker; an element is the complete structure (tags + content).

items.title: 13. A Complete Example
items.text:
Let's unpack this:

<p class="introduction">
    Welcome to <strong>HTML</strong>!
</p>

<p class="introduction">
│ │
│ └── Attribute
│
└── Element name

Welcome to
│
└── Text content

<strong>
│
└── Nested element

HTML
│
└── Content of the <strong> element

</strong>
│
└── Closing tag of the nested element

</p>
│
└── Closing tag of the paragraph

The outer wrapper is the paragraph:

<p class="introduction">
    ...
</p>

Inside it sits:

<strong>HTML</strong>

Nested, tidy, and each bit has a job.

items.title: 14. The General Structure to Remember
items.text:
For most elements you'll use:

<element attribute="value">
    Content
</element>

Like:

<p class="intro">
    Welcome to my website.
</p>

Where:

<p>                 Element name
class="intro"       Attribute
Welcome...          Content
</p>                Closing tag

Void elements are the exception:

<element attribute="value">

Example:

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo">

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Think of it like this:

Opening tag
     ↓
<element attribute="value">
     ↓
Content
     ↓
Closing tag
     ↓
</element>

E.g.:

<p class="intro">Hello, world!</p>

Quick recap:

Part What it does Opening tag Kicks the element off Element name Says what kind of element it is Attribute Adds extra info Attribute value The value for that attribute Content Whatever's inside Closing tag Wraps it up

If you remember one line, make it this:

Tags are the brackets. Elements are the meaningful chunks those brackets create.

items.title: Basic Structure of an HTML Page
items.text: You'll spend a lot of time inside this skeleton, so let's get comfortable with it. Every webpage you build starts the same way: a declaration up top, one root element holding everything, a bit of invisible setup, and then the visible content.

items.title: The full template
items.text:
Keep this handy, you'll want it at the top of every page you create:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Your Page Title</title>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Your page content -->
</body>
</html>

Read it top to bottom; the order actually matters.

items.title: <!DOCTYPE html>: declaration
items.text:
• This first line tells the browser "this is HTML5, so use standards mode." Without it you can end up in quirks mode and wonder why things look odd.
  • It's not a tag, so there's no closing tag and no attributes. It has to be the very first line: nothing above it, not even a comment.
<!DOCTYPE html>

items.title: <html>: root element
items.text:
• Think of <html> as the parent of everything. It wraps <head> and <body>, and its closing tag </html> should be the last line in the file.
  • The lang attribute hints the page language to screen readers and search engines:
<html lang="en">
lang value Meaning en English sw Swahili fr French

items.title: <head>: invisible metadata
items.text:
• <head> holds setup info you don't see on the page itself: the tab title, character set, viewport hint, CSS links, JS, and so on. It's the first child of <html> and always comes before <body>.
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bakery</title>
</head>
Tag inside <head> What it does <title> Tab/window title: also what shows up in search results <meta charset="utf-8"> Character encoding: just include it, always <meta name="viewport" …> Tells mobile browsers how to scale the page: also always include it

items.title: <body>: what visitors actually see
items.text:
• Headings, paragraphs, lists, images, links: if it's visible, it lives in <body>. Each page has exactly one <body>, and it's the second child of <html>.
<body>
  <h1>Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
</body>
The structure of an HTML page

items.title: Hierarchy (who's inside who)
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>      declaration, comes first, owns nothing
<html>               PARENT, wraps everything
  <head>             1st child, invisible setup
  <body>             2nd child, all visible content
  • <html> is the parent; <head> and <body> are its children.
  • <head> always comes before <body>. No visible content goes in <head>: though <title> will show up on the browser tab.

items.title: A few ground rules
items.text:
• One <!DOCTYPE>, one <html>, one <head>, and one <body> per page: no extras.
  • Close tags in reverse order. The <html> you opened second? It closes last.
  • Skip <meta charset> and non-English characters can turn to gibberish. Skip the viewport tag and your layout will look broken on phones. We've all been there.

items.title: Quick recap
items.text: Order Tag Role 1st <!DOCTYPE html> Declaration 2nd <html lang> Root parent 3rd <head> Invisible metadata 4th <body> Visible content

items.title: The Basic Structure of an HTML Element
items.text:
HTML pages are built from elements, labelled chunks that tell the browser what each piece of content means and how it should be structured.

Here's a paragraph element:

<p>Hello, world!</p>

Simple enough, but there are a few moving parts worth naming.

items.text:

<p>Hello, world!</p>

<p>        Hello, world!        </p>

Together, those three make an element.

items.text:
This tells the browser "start here."

<p>

<   p   >
│   │   │
│   │   └── Closing angle bracket
│   └────── Element name
└────────── Opening angle bracket
An opening tag

That name in the middle is the important bit:

<p>
→ paragraph.

<h1>
→ main heading.

<strong>
→ strongly important, not just "make it bold".

items.text:
Whatever lives between the tags.

<p>Hello, world!</p>

Content:

Hello, world!

Another:

<h1>Learning HTML</h1>

Content:

Learning HTML

And it doesn't have to be plain text, elements can hold other elements too:

<p>
    This is <strong>very important</strong> information.
</p>

That paragraph contains text and a <strong> element.

items.text:
This says "we're done."

</p>

See the /? That's the clue.

<p>
vs.

</p>

That slash marks it as the closing tag:

│   │   │
│   │   └── Closing angle bracket
│   └────── Element name
└────────── Opening angle bracket

and for the closer:

<   /   p   >
│   │   │   │
│   │   │   └── Closing angle bracket
│   │   └────── Element name
│   └────────── Forward slash
└────────────── Opening angle bracket

items.text:
Put them together:

<p>Hello, world!</p>

<p>          → Opening tag

Hello, world! → Content

</p>         → Closing tag

In shorthand:

Opening tag + Content + Closing tag = Element

items.title: 6. Another Example
items.text:
<h1>My Website</h1>

That breaks down to:

  • <h1> → opening tag
  • My Website → content
  • </h1> → closing tag
  • the whole thing → HTML element

One more:

<strong>Important information</strong>

<strong>                 Opening tag
Important information    Content
</strong>                Closing tag

items.title: 7. Elements Can Contain Other Elements
items.text:
Elements inside other elements, that's nesting.

<p>
    This is <strong>important</strong> information.
</p>

<strong> lives inside <p>. As a little tree:

<p>
│
├── This is
│
├── <strong>
│   └── important
│
└── information.

That's how simple pieces combine into more interesting pages.

items.title: 8. Proper Nesting
items.text:
Close in the right order. Think of packing boxes, you close the inner one before the outer one.

This is fine:

<p>
    This is <strong>important</strong> information.
</p>

This isn't:

<p>
    This is <strong>important</p> information</strong>

The tags overlap, browsers will guess, but don't make them.

A rule of thumb you'll hear a lot:

Last opened, first closed.

E.g.:

<p>
    <strong>
        Important text
    </strong>
</p>

We opened <strong> last, so we close it first.

items.title: 9. Attributes
items.text:
Attributes add extra info to an element:

<a href="https://example.com">Visit Example</a>

Start from the bare element:

<a>Visit Example</a>

Add the detail to the opening tag:

<a href="https://example.com">

Breakdown:

<a
│
└── Element name

href
│
└── Attribute name

"https://example.com"
│
└── Attribute value
HTML attributes on the opening tag

General shape:

<element attribute="value">
    Content
</element>

E.g.:

<a href="https://example.com">
    Visit Example
</a>

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A sleeping cat" width="400">

src   → cat.jpg
alt   → A sleeping cat
width → 400

<input>
<meta>
<link>

<p>Hello</p>

<p>

and:

</p>

The element is the whole bundle:

<p>Hello</p>

A tag is a marker; an element is the complete structure (tags + content).

items.text:
<p class="introduction">
    Welcome to <strong>HTML</strong>!
</p>

Unpacked:

<p class="introduction">
│ │
│ └── Attribute
│
└── Element name

Welcome to
│
└── Text content

<strong>
│
└── Nested element

HTML
│
└── Content of the <strong> element

</strong>
│
└── Closing tag of the nested element

</p>
│
└── Closing tag of the paragraph

Outer wrapper is the paragraph:

<p class="introduction">
    ...
</p>

Inside it:

<strong>HTML</strong>

Each bit has a clear job.

<element attribute="value">

Opening tag

Content

<p class="intro">Hello, world!</p>

items.title: What Are Headings?
items.text:
Headings are how we introduce and organize sections on a page. Think of them as the outline you'd scribble before writing an essay, just baked into HTML.

There are six of them:

<h1>Heading 1</h1>
<h2>Heading 2</h2>
<h3>Heading 3</h3>
<h4>Heading 4</h4>
<h5>Heading 5</h5>
<h6>Heading 6</h6>

<h1> is the top-level heading, <h6> the deepest. Most pages live happily on just the first two or three.

items.title: 1. The <h1>: main heading
items.text:
<h1> is the big picture, what the whole page is about.

<h1>Introduction to HTML</h1>

A typical start might be:

<h1>Introduction to HTML</h1>

<p>
    HTML is the language used to structure content on the web.
</p>

That <h1> tells anyone skimming (and any screen reader) what they're about to read.

items.title: 2. The <h2>: major sections
items.text:
<h2> breaks the main topic into big chunks.

<h1>Introduction to HTML</h1>

<h2>HTML Elements</h2>

<p>
    HTML elements are the building blocks of webpages.
</p>

<h2>HTML Attributes</h2>

<p>
    Attributes provide additional information about HTML elements.
</p>

Visualised:

Introduction to HTML
│
├── HTML Elements
│
└── HTML Attributes

So <h1> is the book title; <h2>s are the chapter titles.

items.title: 3. The <h3>: subsections
items.text:
Need to go deeper under an <h2>? That's <h3>.

<h1>Introduction to HTML</h1>

<h2>HTML Elements</h2>

<p>
    HTML elements provide structure to webpages.
</p>

<h3>Headings</h3>

<p>
    Headings are used to organize sections of content.
</p>

<h3>Paragraphs</h3>

<p>
    Paragraphs contain blocks of text.
</p>

Hierarchy:

Introduction to HTML       <h1>
│
└── HTML Elements          <h2>
    │
    ├── Headings           <h3>
    │
    └── Paragraphs         <h3>

items.title: 4. <h4>, <h5>, and <h6>: when you really need depth
items.text:
They work the same way, just deeper:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h2>Frontend Development</h2>

<h3>HTML</h3>

<h4>Text Elements</h4>

<h5>Emphasis</h5>

<h6>Strong Importance</h6>

Web Development              h1
│
└── Frontend Development     h2
    │
    └── HTML                 h3
        │
        └── Text Elements    h4
            │
            └── Emphasis     h5
                │
                └── Strong Importance  h6

Honestly, most sites you'll build at Migadde will use <h1>–<h3> and stop there. The lower levels are for docs with a lot of nesting.

items.title: 5. Headings Are About Hierarchy, Not Size
items.text:
It's tempting to pick headings because "h2 looks nice and big." Don't.

They describe how sections relate, not how big the text should be.

<h1>Learning Web Development</h1>

<h2>HTML</h2>

<h3>Elements</h3>

<h3>Attributes</h3>

<h2>CSS</h2>

<h3>Selectors</h3>

<h3>Properties</h3>

That means:

Learning Web Development
│
├── HTML
│   ├── Elements
│   └── Attributes
│
└── CSS
    ├── Selectors
    └── Properties

The levels carry the structure, even if CSS later makes them all look similar.

items.title: 6. Headings + Paragraphs
items.text:
Usually a heading introduces whatever paragraphs follow it:

<h2>HTML Tables</h2>

<p>
    Tables allow us to organize information into rows and columns.
</p>

<p>
    A table can contain headings, rows, and individual data cells.
</p>

HTML Tables
    ↓
Paragraph
    ↓
Paragraph

The heading sets expectations; the paragraphs deliver.

items.title: 7. Don't Pick a Heading for Its Size
items.text:
We've all done this:

<h3>This is a big title</h3>

...just because we liked how <h3> looks by default. Use the level that matches the structure instead:

<h1>Main Heading</h1>
for the page title,

<h2>Major Section</h2>
for a section beneath it,

<h3>Subsection</h3>
for something inside that section.

Want it bigger or smaller? That's CSS's job:

h2 {
    font-size: 2rem;
}

items.title: 8. Try Not to Skip Levels
items.text:
This isn't invalid, but it usually means the outline wasn't thought through:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h3>HTML</h3>

There's an <h2> missing in between. Clearer:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h2>HTML</h2>

And if HTML itself has sub-topics:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h2>HTML</h2>

<h3>Elements</h3>

<h3>Attributes</h3>

Think hierarchy, not font-size ladder.

items.title: 9. You Don't Have to Use Every Level
items.text:
This is perfectly fine:

<h1>My Website</h1>

<h2>About Me</h2>

<h2>Projects</h2>

<h2>Contact</h2>

No <h3> needed if there are no subsections. Let the content dictate the levels.

items.title: 10. A Real-World Example
items.text:
Say we're putting together a page about Python:

<h1>Learning Python</h1>

<p>
    Python is a general-purpose programming language used in many areas
    of software development.
</p>

<h2>Python Basics</h2>

<p>
    Python provides several fundamental features that beginners should
    understand.
</p>

<h3>Variables</h3>

<p>
    Variables allow programs to store and work with values.
</p>

<h3>Functions</h3>

<p>
    Functions allow us to organize reusable pieces of code.
</p>

<h2>Object-Oriented Programming</h2>

<p>
    Python supports object-oriented programming through classes and objects.
</p>

<h3>Classes</h3>

<p>
    Classes provide a way to define the structure and behaviour of objects.
</p>

Structure:

Learning Python                 h1
│
├── Python Basics               h2
│   ├── Variables               h3
│   └── Functions               h3
│
└── Object-Oriented Programming h2
    └── Classes                 h3

Much more meaningful than just making some text bigger than other text.

items.title: 11. Headings Help Everyone Navigate: Especially Screen Readers
items.text:
A screen reader can pull out your headings and let a user jump between:

About Us
Services
Products
Contact

That's only useful if the headings reflect the actual structure, not just visual styling. So it's both a design and an accessibility habit.

items.title: 12. Headings vs Page Titles
items.text:
They look similar but do different jobs.

In <head>:

<head>
    <title>Learning HTML</title>
</head>

Visible on the page:

<body>
    <h1>Learning HTML</h1>
</body>
  • <title> describes the document for the browser tab and search results: you won't see it in the page body.
  • <h1> is the visible headline for readers on the page itself.

items.title: Quick Reference
Headings h1–h6 Showcase
items.text: You'll meet all six heading levels here and see how they stack up, not just how big they look, but when you'd actually reach for each one.

items.title: The rule to carry with you
items.text: Every page should have one <h1>, that's the page's title. And don't skip levels just because you like the default size (jumping straight from <h1> to <h3> is a giveaway you picked for looks, not structure).

items.title: All six levels
items.text: Tag Rough default look When you'd use it <h1> Bakery Homepage (largest) Page title: once per page <h2> Our Menu Major sections <h3> Drinks Subsections inside an h2 <h4> Hot Drinks Deeper nesting <h5> Tea Notes Fine detail you'll rarely need <h6> Fine print head (smallest) Deepest level, used sparingly

items.title: Snippets
items.text:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<h3>Drinks</h3>
<h4>Hot Drinks</h4>
<h5>Tea Notes</h5>
<h6>Fine print head</h6>

Here's what correct nesting looks like, no levels skipped:

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<h3>Drinks</h3>
<h2>Prices</h2>

<h2> → <h3> is fine; <h1> → <h3> without an <h2> isn't ideal.

items.title: A few habits to avoid
items.text:
• Two <h1>s on one page? Split it into two pages or demote one to <h2>.
  • <h1> followed immediately by <h3>? Slip in that missing <h2>: even if it feels a bit redundant.
  • A paragraph styled to look huge is not a heading. Screen readers won't list it, and your outline breaks.
Headings

items.title: Quick recap
items.text: Level Size hint Role h1 Biggest Page title, once h2 Large Sections h3–h6 Shrinking Subsections: don't skip

items.title: What Are Paragraphs?
items.text:
Paragraphs are blocks of thought, one idea per block. That's it. It's the default way we chunk text on the web:

<p>Fresh bread baked every morning.</p>
  • Block-level: Each <p> starts on a new line, and browsers add a little breathing room above and below automatically.
  • Readability: One idea per <p>. Short paragraphs scan so much better on a phone than a wall of text: try reading both and you'll feel it.

items.title: <p> vs <br>
items.text:
• <p> starts a new thought: a new block.
  • <br> just breaks the line inside the same thought: handy for an address, a poem, or a signature block, not for essays:
<p>Line one<br>Line two, same thought</p>
Paragraphs

Don't be tempted to stack breaks like <br><br><br> to fake paragraph spacing, it's the classic lab slip-up we see at Migadde. Use <p> plus CSS margins instead. Stacked breaks carry no meaning for screen readers, either.

items.title: <hr> = thematic break
items.text:
<hr> signals a scene change, when a story jumps to a new scene, or a menu flips to prices:

<p>Menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices</p>

It happens to render as a horizontal line, but its job is semantic: "topic shifts here." Not decoration.

items.title: Quick habits
items.text:
1. One idea per <p>, keep them short.
  2. <br> is an empty tag (no closing tag), use it sparingly, inside a paragraph.
  3. <hr> is also empty, it marks a shift in topic, not a pretty divider.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Meaning Empty? p Block of thought No br Line break within the same thought Yes hr Thematic break Yes

items.title: Paragraphs, Breaks, Rules (Syntax)
items.text: Here's the exact syntax for p, br, and hr, nothing extra.

items.title: <p>: paragraph
items.text:
p wraps a block of thought. Spacing above and below is added for you:

<p>Fresh bread baked daily.</p>

items.title: <br>: line break
items.text:
Empty tag, so no closing tag. It just breaks the line inside the same paragraph:

<p>Line one<br>Line two</p>

Renders as:

Line one Line two

items.title: <hr>: thematic break
items.text:
Also an empty tag, no closing tag. It signals a shift in topic between blocks:

<p>Menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices</p>

items.title: A couple of guardrails
items.text:
• A <br> inside a heading can be okay for a two-line title, but never use it for vertical spacing: that's what CSS margins are for.
  • Seeing several <hr>s in a row? That's usually a hint you actually want headings instead.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Closing tag? Job p Yes, </p> Block of thought br No Line break within the same thought hr No Thematic break

items.title: Combined: Headings + Paragraphs in the Basic Structure
items.text: Headings and paragraphs do the heavy lifting for text on most pages. A heading names the section, a paragraph says something about it. The trick is using them together so the document actually makes sense.

items.title: 1. A Heading Followed by a Paragraph
items.text:
The simplest combo:

<h1>Learning HTML</h1>

<p>
    HTML is the language used to structure content on the web.
</p>

Here:

  • <h1> names the topic.
  • <p> gives you the detail.

Browsers will render the heading bigger and bolder and put the paragraph underneath, but you're choosing them for meaning, not just looks.

items.title: 2. Multiple Paragraphs Under One Heading
items.text:
One heading can comfortably introduce several paragraphs:

<h1>Learning HTML</h1>

<p>
    HTML is used to structure content on webpages.
</p>

<p>
    It provides elements for headings, paragraphs, links,
    images, tables, forms, and many other types of content.
</p>

Both paragraphs sit under that <h1>. When you feel yourself starting a new idea or point, that's your cue for a new <p>, don't cram everything into one long block.

items.title: 3. Using Different Heading Levels
items.text:
Six levels are available:

<h1>...</h1>
<h2>...</h2>
<h3>...</h3>
<h4>...</h4>
<h5>...</h5>
<h6>...</h6>

They signal how deep you are in the outline. For instance:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<p>
    Web development involves creating websites and web applications.
</p>

<h2>HTML</h2>

<p>
    HTML is used to structure the content of a webpage.
</p>

<h2>CSS</h2>

<p>
    CSS is used to control the appearance of a webpage.
</p>

<h2>JavaScript</h2>

<p>
    JavaScript is used to add behaviour and interactivity.
</p>

Visualised:

Web Development
│
├── HTML
│
├── CSS
│
└── JavaScript

<h1> is the main topic; each <h2> is a major section inside it.

items.title: 4. Adding Subsections
items.text:
You can nest sections further:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<p>
    Web development involves building websites and web applications.
</p>

<h2>Frontend Development</h2>

<p>
    Frontend development focuses on the parts of a website that users
    see and interact with.
</p>

<h3>HTML</h3>

<p>
    HTML provides the structure of the webpage.
</p>

<h3>CSS</h3>

<p>
    CSS controls the appearance of the webpage.
</p>

<h2>Backend Development</h2>

<p>
    Backend development deals with servers, databases, APIs, and
    application logic.
</p>

Hierarchy:

Web Development              <h1>
│
├── Frontend Development     <h2>
│   │
│   ├── HTML                 <h3>
│   │
│   └── CSS                  <h3>
│
└── Backend Development      <h2>

Heading levels are how you communicate that nesting to browsers and assistive tech.

items.title: 5. A Heading Should Say What Comes Next
items.text:
Make it descriptive. Compare:

Good:

<h2>HTML Tables</h2>

<p>
    HTML tables allow us to organize information into rows and columns.
</p>

Also good:

<h2>Creating Links</h2>

<p>
    The anchor element is used to create hyperlinks between webpages.
</p>

In both cases the reader knows immediately what the paragraph will cover. If your heading could sit above any paragraph, it's probably too vague.

items.title: 6. Don't Use Headings Just to Make Text Bigger
items.text:
It's a common slip, we like how <h2> looks, so we wrap any large text in it:

<h2>Welcome to my website</h2>

If that's just a normal line you want styled large, it shouldn't be a heading. Headings are for document structure. Let CSS handle looks:

<p class="large-text">Welcome to my website</p>

.large-text {
    font-size: 2rem;
}

items.title: 7. Don't Skip Levels for Appearance
items.text:
This jumps over <h2>:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h3>HTML</h3>

Stick to the logical order instead:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h2>HTML</h2>

And if HTML itself has sub-topics:

<h1>Web Development</h1>

<h2>HTML</h2>

<h3>Elements</h3>

<h3>Attributes</h3>

<h3>Forms</h3>

It's about hierarchy that makes sense, not making each heading a little smaller.

items.title: 8. One <h1> for the Main Topic
items.text:
For a simple page:

<h1>Introduction to Python</h1>

<p>
    Python is a general-purpose programming language known for its
    readable syntax.
</p>

<h2>Variables</h2>

<p>
    Variables allow us to store and work with values in a program.
</p>

<h2>Functions</h2>

<p>
    Functions allow us to organize reusable pieces of code.
</p>

<h2>Classes</h2>

<p>
    Classes provide a way to model objects and organize related data
    and behaviour.
</p>

Think of <h1> as the document title; <h2>s divide that title into sections.

items.title: 9. Headings and Paragraphs Build the Whole Document
items.text:
You'll reuse this pattern everywhere:

<h1>Main Topic</h1>

<p>Introduction to the main topic.</p>

<h2>First Section</h2>

<p>Information about the first section.</p>

<p>More information about the first section.</p>

<h2>Second Section</h2>

<p>Information about the second section.</p>

<h3>Subsection</h3>

<p>More specific information about the second section.</p>

That repetition is a feature, once you see it, pages become easier to skim, and browsers, search engines and screen readers can build a better map of your content.

items.title: 10. A Real-World Example: Uganda
items.text:
Say you're putting together a quick info page:

<h1>Uganda</h1>

<p>
    Uganda is a country in East Africa known for its diverse landscapes,
    wildlife, and cultures.
</p>

<h2>Geography</h2>

<p>
    Uganda is located in East Africa and has a landscape that includes
    lakes, mountains, forests, and savannahs.
</p>

<h2>Wildlife</h2>

<p>
    Uganda is home to many species of wildlife, including elephants,
    lions, chimpanzees, and mountain gorillas.
</p>

<h3>Mountain Gorillas</h3>

<p>
    Mountain gorillas can be found in the forests of southwestern Uganda.
</p>

<h2>Culture</h2>

<p>
    Uganda has many different cultural groups, languages, traditions,
    and forms of artistic expression.
</p>

Structure:

Uganda
│
├── Geography
│
├── Wildlife
│   │
│   └── Mountain Gorillas
│
└── Culture

You're not just displaying text, you're describing how the pieces relate.

items.title: Quick Rule of Thumb
items.text:
Ask yourself:

Heading → What is this section about?

Paragraph → What do I want to say about it?

E.g.:

<h2>HTML Forms</h2>

<p>
    HTML forms allow users to enter and submit information to a website.
</p>

Heading names it; paragraph explains it.

items.title: Meaning vs Looks: The Core Rule
items.text:
HTML has several ways to make text stand out, but they aren't interchangeable. Some tell the browser and screen reader what the text means; others just change how it looks. Get this distinction right and most of your other choices get easier.

HTML is about meaning first, looks second.

So if something is genuinely important, you'd reach for <strong>. If you only want it to look bold without implying importance, you'd use <b>. Same story with <em> vs <i>. Let's see why that matters.

items.title: 1. <strong>: strong importance
items.text:
<strong> says the content has real importance, seriousness or urgency, not just "make it bold."

<p>
    <strong>Warning:</strong> This action cannot be undone.
</p>

Yes, browsers usually render it bold. But the bold is a side effect; the meaning is the point. "Warning" deserves attention, so <strong> fits.

Another:

<p>
    You <strong>must</strong> save your work before closing the application.
</p>

That "must" changes what the reader should do.

items.title: Why we call it semantic
items.text:
A semantic element describes what content means, not what it looks like.

<strong>Important:</strong>

doesn't mean

Make this text bold.

It means

This text has strong importance.

That nuance helps with accessibility, screen readers, search engines, maintainability, and it keeps your CSS honest later on.

items.title: Don't use <strong> just because you want bold
items.text:
Browsers render it bold by default, but that shouldn't drive the decision:

<p>
    The price is <strong>50,000 UGX</strong>.
</p>

If 50,000 UGX isn't actually urgent or important in context, <strong> is the wrong signal, even if you like the bold look. For pure styling, CSS is usually a better fit.

items.title: 2. <b>: draw attention, no extra importance
items.text:
<b> also looks bold by default, but it doesn't claim the text is more important.

<p>
    Welcome to the <b>HTML Fundamentals</b> course.
</p>

"HTML Fundamentals" stands out visually, but we're not saying it's more important than everything else in that sentence, just noticeable.

items.title: How <b> differs from <strong>
items.text:
<p>
    <strong>Warning:</strong> The server is offline.
</p>
→ communicates importance.

<p>
    Learn <b>HTML</b>, CSS, and JavaScript.
</p>
→ draws the eye to "HTML" without adding importance.

Quick mental check:

Element What you're saying <strong> This matters a lot <b> Look here, but it's not "more important"

Both may render bold, yet they mean different things.

items.title: 3. <em>: emphasis
items.text:
<em> is for emphasis that changes how a sentence is read. Browsers usually show it italic.

<p>
    You should <em>always</em> test your code.
</p>

"always" gets stress, it alters the intended reading.

items.title: Emphasis can shift meaning entirely
items.text:
<p>
    I said you should submit the assignment.
</p>

Now stress different words:

<p>
    <em>I</em> said you should submit the assignment.
</p>
→ I said it (not someone else).

<p>
    I said <em>you</em> should submit the assignment.
</p>
→ you should do it.

<p>
    I said you should <em>submit</em> the assignment.
</p>
→ the action matters.

That tiny italic can change interpretation, which is exactly why <em> carries meaning.

items.title: 4. <i>: text set apart, not emphasized
items.text:
<i> is for text that should be set apart from its surroundings without implying emphasis or importance. It also renders italic by default.

<p>
    The scientific name is <i>Homo sapiens</i>.
</p>

Scientific names are conventionally italic.

<p>
    The word <i>bonjour</i> is French.
</p>

Foreign words are visually differentiated, same idea.

items.title: Not just "make it italic"
items.text: <i> covers things like technical terms, foreign words, taxonomic names, thoughts, or any phrase that's conventionally displayed differently. If you only want italics for decoration, CSS is usually cleaner.

items.title: 5. <em> vs <i>: same look, different intent
items.text:
Both go italic, but ask why you're marking it up.

<em>: emphasis:

<p>
    You should <em>really</em> read this chapter.
</p>
"really" is stressed.

<i>: set apart:

<p>
    The word <i>computer</i> comes from Latin roots.
</p>
We're presenting the term differently, not stressing it.

Element Purpose Default look <em> Emphasis Italic <i> Text set apart Italic

Looks can fool you, meaning is what splits them.

items.title: 6. <mark>: highlighted because it's relevant right now
items.text:
<mark> highlights text that's relevant in the current context. Browsers usually give it a yellowish background.

<p>
    Search results for <mark>Python</mark>
</p>

"Python" is highlighted because it matched the search, not because it's universally important.

Other contexts:

<p>
    The exam will cover <mark>HTML forms</mark> and tables.
</p>

<p>
    Remember to bring your <mark>student ID</mark> to the examination.
</p>

In each case, you're drawing the reader's eye to what's pertinent here and now.

items.title: <mark> vs <strong>
items.text:
• <strong> → "This is important." E.g. <strong>Do not share your password.</strong>
  • <mark> → "This is relevant/highlighted here." E.g. Your search found <mark>25 results</mark>.

Highlighting isn't importance; importance isn't just highlighting.

items.title: <strong> vs <b>
items.text:
<p>
    <strong>Warning:</strong> Your account will be deleted.
</p>
That's urgent, <strong>.

<p>
    Learn <b>Python</b> with practical projects.
</p>
That's visually distinct, <b>.

Rule of thumb: - Importance → <strong>, eye-catcher without importance → <b>.

items.title: <em> vs <i>
items.text:
<p>
    You should <em>carefully</em> read the instructions.
</p>
Emphasis → <em>.

<p>
    The French word <i>bonjour</i> means hello.
</p>
Set apart → <i>.

Rule of thumb: - Want vocal stress? <em>. Need a different voice or convention? <i>.

items.title: 8. You Can Combine Them: Sparingly
items.text:
When both meanings really apply, nesting is fine:

<p>
    <strong>
        <em>Important:</em>
        Save your work before continuing.
    </strong>
</p>
<strong> = important. <em> = emphasis on "Important".

Highlight plus importance is also okay when both are true:

<p>
    <mark><strong>Deadline: Friday</strong></mark>
</p>

Just don't stack them to make text look "more dramatic." If there's no meaning behind it, leave it out.

items.title: 9. Appearance Isn't the Point
items.text:
By default you'll see:

<strong>Important</strong>
<b>Bold</b>
<em>Emphasized</em>
<i>Italic</i>
<mark>Highlighted</mark>

Roughly:

  • <strong> → bold
  • <b> → bold
  • <em> → italic
  • <i> → italic
  • <mark> → highlighted background

So <strong> and <b> can look identical, same for <em>/<i>. That's exactly why you shouldn't choose based on looks.

items.title: 10. Let CSS Handle Looks
items.text:
HTML says what something is; CSS decides how it looks. So you can keep the meaning and change the presentation:

<strong class="warning">Warning</strong>

.warning {
    color: red;
    font-weight: normal;
}
It's still "strong importance," even if it's no longer bold.

Likewise, you can make normal text look bold without <b>:

<p class="important">Important information</p>

.important {
    font-weight: bold;
}

Separating meaning from appearance is the habit that scales.

items.title: 11. Common Mix-Ups
items.text:
"I want bold, so <b> everywhere." If "Warning" is actually important, prefer <strong>Warning</strong>.

"I want italic, so <i> everywhere." If you mean vocal emphasis, You *must* read this, use <em>You must read this carefully.</em>.

"My favourite language is Python: I'll just strong it." 

<p>
    My favorite language is <strong>Python</strong>.
</p>
If "Python" isn't especially important in context, bolding it with <strong> muddies the signal. Consider <b> or CSS.

"<mark> for warnings." 

<mark>WARNING: Do not delete this file.</mark>
That's importance, not highlighting. Reach for <strong> (and add <mark> only if highlighting is also relevant).

items.title: 12. Putting It All Together
items.text:
<p>
    <strong>Important:</strong>
    You should <em>always</em> back up your files.
    The term <i>backup</i> refers to an additional copy of your data.
    <mark>Remember to test your backups.</mark>
</p>
  • <strong>Important:</strong>: strong importance.
  • <em>always</em>: vocal emphasis.
  • <i>backup</i>: term set apart.
  • <mark>Remember to test your backups.</mark>: relevant and worth highlighting now.

Each choice signals something a browser or screen reader can actually use.

items.title: 13. Quick Reference
items.text: Element Meaning Typical look Reach for it when <strong> Strong importance Bold Something is important or urgent <b> Attention without added importance Bold You need visual distinction but no extra semantics <em> Emphasis Italic You'd stress the word when speaking <i> Text set apart Italic Term needs a different voice or convention <mark> Highlighted relevance Highlighted It's relevant or noteworthy in this context

items.title: 14. The Main Idea
items.text:
Don't pick these tags by how they render. Ask what the text means:

Is it important or urgent?
        ↓
    <strong>

Does it need vocal stress?
        ↓
       <em>

Just need to draw the eye without implying importance?
        ↓
        <b>

Is it a term or phrase set apart by convention?
        ↓
        <i>

Is it being highlighted because it's relevant right now?
        ↓
      <mark>

The browser's default styling is just a starting point. Semantic HTML describes what your content is; CSS can decide how it looks.

items.title: Code Family
items.text: When you're writing about code, you want the markup to say "this is code", not just look monospace. HTML gives you a little family of elements for that.

items.title: 1. Inline Code
items.text:
<code> is for a short snippet inside a sentence:

<p>
    Use the <code>print()</code> function to display text in Python.
</p>

Browsers typically render it in a monospace font, but the real win is semantics, tools know it's code.

items.title: 2. Code Blocks
items.text:
For multiple lines, pair <pre> with <code>:

<pre><code>
name = "Jonathan"
print(name)
</code></pre>

<pre> keeps your spaces and line breaks exactly as typed; <code> says "this is code."

items.title: 3. Preserving Formatting with <pre>
items.text:
On its own, <pre> is the one element that respects your whitespace:

<pre>
Name: Jonathan
Age: 27
Country: Uganda
</pre>

What you type is what you get, line breaks and indentation included.

items.title: 4. What About Showing HTML Itself?
items.text:
Browsers normally interpret tags. So this:

<p>Hello World</p>

would render as a paragraph, not as visible code. To show the tags as text, escape them:

<pre><code>
<p>Hello World</p>
</code></pre>

That displays as:

<p>Hello World</p>

Handy when you're writing tutorials (like this one!).

items.title: 5. Keyboard Input
items.text:
<kbd> marks keys you press:

<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save the file.</p>

Great for instructions and shortcuts, screen readers can also announce it more meaningfully than plain text.

items.title: 6. Program Output
items.text:
<samp> is for sample output from a program:

<p>
    The program returned:
    <samp>Hello, World!</samp>
</p>

It says "this is what the computer printed."

items.title: 7. Variables
items.text:
<var> marks a variable in maths or code:

<p>The area of a rectangle is <var>width</var> × <var>height</var>.</p>

items.title: At a glance
items.text: Element When to reach for it <code> Inline code <pre> Preserve spaces and line breaks <kbd> Keyboard input <samp> Sample output from a program <var> A variable in an expression

items.title: Tiny Semantics: Big Meaning
items.text: Some of the smallest tags do the most useful work. They don't change much visually, but they tell browsers, screen readers and search engines what your text actually is.

items.title: <abbr>: Abbreviation
items.text:
<abbr> marks an abbreviation or acronym. Pair it with title to give the full expansion:

<p>I am learning <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>.</p>

Browsers often show the title as a tooltip on hover, and assistive tech can use it too.

Another:

<p>
    The <abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr>
    provides health information around the world.
</p>

items.title: <time>: Date and Time
items.text:
<time> flags a specific date, time or period.

<p>The class starts at <time>9:00 AM</time>.</p>

For a date:

<p>The event is on <time>2026-10-07</time>.</p>

Want to be machine-readable as well as human-friendly? Add datetime:

<p>
    PyCon Africa starts on
    <time datetime="2026-10-07">October 7, 2026</time>.
</p>

Humans read "October 7, 2026"; computers parse 2026-10-07.

items.title: <del>: Deleted Text
items.text:
<del> means text that's been removed:

<p>
    The price is <del>50,000</del> 40,000 shillings.
</p>

Browsers usually strike it through.

items.title: <ins>: Inserted Text
items.text:
<ins> is the counterpart, text that's been added:

<p>
    The price is <del>50,000</del> <ins>40,000</ins> shillings.
</p>

Useful when you're showing edits or price changes.

items.title: <sub>: Subscript
items.text:
<sub> sits below the baseline, think chemistry:

<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>

Also handy for maths:

<p>x<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub></p>

items.title: <sup>: Superscript
items.text:
<sup> sits above the baseline, exponents, ordinals:

<p>2<sup>3</sup> = 8</p>

<p>1<sup>st</sup> place</p>

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Element What it means <abbr> Abbreviation or acronym <time> Date or time <del> Deleted content <ins> Inserted content <sub> Subscript <sup> Superscript

Tiny elements, but they add real semantic meaning, not just a visual tweak.

items.title: Quotes
items.text: HTML makes a useful distinction between a quick quote inside a sentence and a longer passage set apart. It also gives you a clean way to say where a quote came from.

items.title: 1. Inline Quotes
items.text:
<q> is for a short quotation inside a sentence:

<p>
    Albert Einstein said, <q>Imagination is more important than knowledge.</q>
</p>

Browsers typically wrap it in quotation marks for you, no need to type them by hand.

items.title: 2. Block Quotes
items.text:
For a longer quotation that stands on its own, use <blockquote>:

<blockquote>
    The important thing is not to stop questioning.
    Curiosity has its own reason for existing.
</blockquote>

Browsers usually indent block quotes to set them apart.

items.title: 3. Citing the Source
items.text:
You can attach a source URL directly to <blockquote> with cite:

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/article">
    The important thing is not to stop questioning.
</blockquote>

That cite attribute won't be visible on the page, but it's there for tools that want it.

items.title: 4. The <cite> Element
items.text:
<cite> identifies the title of a work, a book, film, song, article:

<p>
    My favourite book is <cite>Things Fall Apart</cite>.
</p>

You can use it for attributions too:

<blockquote>
    The world is a fine place and worth fighting for.
</blockquote>

<p>
    Source: <cite>Ernest Hemingway</cite>
</p>

items.title: 5. <q> vs <blockquote>: Which One?
Special Blocks
items.text: Three block tags you'll use less often, but when you need them, nothing else will do: one for exact whitespace, one for contact info, and one for fine print.

items.title: <pre>: preformatted text
items.text:
pre is the only element that keeps spaces and line breaks exactly as you type them. That's why it's the home for multi-line code:

<pre>line 1
  indented line 2</pre>

If you want a code block that also says "this is code," pair it with <code>:

<pre><code>def hello():
    print("hi")</code></pre>

items.title: <address>: contact info
items.text:
address holds contact information for the author or owner of the page or section, not just any postal address that happens to appear in your text:

<address>hello@mhsm.web<br>Dar es Salaam</address>

Browsers usually italicise it. You'll typically see it near the footer or an author bio.

items.title: <small>: fine print
items.text:
small is for side comments, copyright, disclaimers, legal notes, attributions:

<small>© 2026 MHSM. All rights reserved.</small>

Browsers render it a touch smaller than normal text. It doesn't make the text unimportant, it just marks it as secondary.

items.title: A few things to watch
items.text:
• Inside <pre> you still need to escape < as <: otherwise the browser thinks it's a tag.
  • <address> shouldn't contain headings or sectioning content: keep it to contact lines.
  • <small> inside <footer> is the classic combo for a copyright line.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Job Watch out pre Exact whitespace Escape < as < address Author/owner contact Not any random address small Fine print Still readable, not hidden

items.title: 1. What are Links?
items.text:
Links are how users jump from one place to another on the web.

HTML uses the <a> element, the anchor, for that:

<a href="about.html">About Us</a>

The text "About Us" is what the visitor actually clicks.

items.title: 2. The <a> Element
items.text:
A hyperlink is just an <a> with a destination:

<a href="https://www.google.com">Google</a>

Breaking it down:

  • <a>: the anchor element
  • href: where it points
  • Google: the clickable label

items.title: 3. The href Attribute
items.text:
href says where the link goes:

<a href="about.html">About Us</a>

That destination could be:

  • another page on your site
  • a page on a different website
  • a spot on the same page
  • an email address

items.title: 4. Linking to Another Website
items.text:
Use the full URL:

<a href="https://www.wikipedia.org">Wikipedia</a>

<a href="https://www.python.org">Python</a>

items.title: 5. Linking to Another Page on Your Site
items.text:
Say your site looks like this:

website/
├── index.html
├── about.html
└── contact.html

From index.html you can point to the others directly:

<a href="about.html">About Us</a>

<a href="contact.html">Contact Us</a>

items.title: 6. Linking to a Page Inside a Folder
items.text:
If the target lives in a folder, include that folder in the path:

website/
├── index.html
└── pages/
    ├── about.html
    └── contact.html

<a href="pages/about.html">About Us</a>

items.title: 7. Opening a Link in a New Tab
items.text:
Want the link to open elsewhere? Add target:

<a href="https://www.python.org" target="_blank">
    Python
</a>

target="_blank" usually opens a new tab, handy for external sites so you don't pull people away from yours.

items.title: 8. Linking to an Email Address
items.text:
Use the mailto: scheme:

<a href="mailto:example@email.com">
    Send me an email
</a>

Clicking it will try to open the visitor's email app.

items.title: 9. Linking to a Specific Spot on a Page
items.text:
Give an element an id first:

<h2 id="contact">Contact Us</h2>

Then link to it with a hash:

<a href="#contact">Go to Contact Us</a>

That # tells the browser "find the element with this id and scroll to it."

items.title: 10. Linking an Image
items.text:
An image can be the clickable thing too:

<a href="about.html">
    <img src="images/logo.png" alt="About Us" width="200">
</a>

Click the image → go to about.html.

items.title: 11. Navigation Links
items.text:
Put those <a>s together and you've got site navigation:

<nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="about.html">About</a>
    <a href="services.html">Services</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

That's how users move between pages, simple, but essential.

items.title: 12. Putting It Together
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My Website</title>
</head>

<body>

    <h1>My Website</h1>

    <nav>
        <a href="index.html">Home</a>
        <a href="about.html">About</a>
        <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
    </nav>

    <h2>Welcome</h2>

    <p>
        Visit the
        <a href="https://www.python.org">Python website</a>
        to learn more about Python.
    </p>

</body>
</html>

items.title: At a glance
items.text: Element / Attribute What it's for <a> Creates a link href Where the link points target Where to open it target="_blank" Open in a new tab/window mailto: Make it an email link #id Jump to an element on the page

items.title: 1. What are Images?
items.text:
Pictures on a page make it more inviting and can explain things words alone can't. HTML uses a single element for that:

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

items.title: 2. The <img> Element
items.text:
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A beautiful landscape">

Notice there's no closing tag, <img> is a void element. It sits there and displays the image.

items.title: 3. The src Attribute
items.text:
src tells the browser where to find the image:

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

In a folder?

<img src="images/cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

Or out on the web:

<img src="https://example.com/cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

items.title: 4. The alt Attribute
items.text:
alt is the text description for the image:

<img src="dog.jpg" alt="A brown dog">

You'll need it when:

  • the image fails to load,
  • someone is using a screen reader,
  • you need a text fallback for any other reason.

Think of it as "what would I say if I had to describe this image over the phone?"

items.title: 5. Image Width and Height
items.text:
width sets the display width:

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat" width="400">

height does the same vertically:

<img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat" width="400" height="300">

You can use one or both, browsers will scale accordingly.

items.title: 6. Images in Folders
items.text:
Most sites keep images tidily in a folder:

website/
├── index.html
└── images/
    ├── cat.jpg
    └── dog.jpg

Referencing cat.jpg from index.html:

<img src="images/cat.jpg" alt="A cat">

items.title: 7. Image Captions
items.text:
A caption is the visible text you see under a picture. HTML pairs <figure> and <figcaption> for that:

<figure>
    <img src="cat.jpg" alt="A sleeping cat">
    <figcaption>A cat sleeping on a chair.</figcaption>
</figure>
  • <figure> groups the image and its caption.
  • <figcaption> holds the caption text itself.

items.title: 8. alt Text vs Caption: Not the Same Job
items.text:
<figure>
    <img src="elephant.jpg" alt="An elephant walking through grass">
    <figcaption>An elephant in Queen Elizabeth National Park.</figcaption>
</figure>
  • alt: functional description, for accessibility and when the image can't be shown.
  • figcaption: visible caption the reader sees alongside the image.

You'll often need both.

items.title: 9. Complete Example
items.text:
<figure>
    <img
        src="images/mountain.jpg"
        alt="A mountain surrounded by trees"
        width="500"
    >

    <figcaption>
        A mountain surrounded by trees.
    </figcaption>
</figure>

items.title: At a glance
items.text: Element / Attribute Role <img> Displays an image src Where the image lives alt Text description width Display width height Display height <figure> Groups image with its caption <figcaption> The visible caption

items.title: Lists
items.text: Lists are how we structure related items, shopping, steps, terms and definitions, without losing the relationship between them.

items.title: <ul>: unordered list
items.text:
ul is a bulleted list where order doesn't matter. Each item is an <li>:

<ul>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
</ul>

items.title: <ol>: ordered list
items.text:
ol is a numbered list where order matters, steps, rankings. The browser numbers them for you:

<ol>
  <li>Mix flour and water.</li>
  <li>Knead ten minutes.</li>
  <li>Bake at 220°C.</li>
</ol>

Need to start elsewhere or count backwards? Use start or reversed:

<ol start="5">
  <li>Fifth step first</li>
</ol>

items.title: Nesting lists
items.text:
An <li> can hold an entire sub-list, and the nested list belongs inside that <li>, not after it:

<ul>
  <li>Bread
    <ul>
      <li>White</li>
      <li>Brown</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Milk</li>
</ul>

That's the pattern you'll see for menus and grouped items.

items.title: <dl>: description list
items.text:
dl handles term + definition pairs, glossaries, menus with descriptions, metadata:

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language, page structure.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets, page styling.</dd>
</dl>
Tag Role dl The whole description list dt Term dd Definition or description

items.title: A few habits to keep
items.text:
• Only <li> may sit directly inside ul or ol: no bare text or <p> wrappers at that level.
  • Don't fake a list with <br> or - dashes. You'll lose count, semantics and accessibility in one go.
  • Navigation menus are just lists: you'll see <nav><ul>… everywhere, so get comfortable with it.

items.title: Recap
items.text: List When to use it Markers ul Order doesn't matter Bullets ol Order matters Numbers, added automatically dl Term → definition None

items.title: Tables
items.text: When you have information that naturally sits in rows and columns, marks, prices, timetables, a table is the right tool. Not for layout, but for data where the row/column relationship matters.

items.title: What counts as tabular data?
items.text:
Think:

  • Student marks
  • Product prices and quantities
  • Class timetables
  • Sales records

For example:

Name Age Class John 15 S2 Sarah 14 S1 David 16 S3

HTML gives you a handful of elements to build exactly that.

items.title: The Basic Table
items.text:
<table> creates the table:

<table>
</table>

Empty, of course. You need rows and cells inside it:

<table>
    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
        <td>14</td>
        <td>S1</td>
    </tr>
</table>

items.title: <tr>: Table Row
items.text:
<tr> is a table row, one horizontal line:

<tr>
</tr>

Two rows, for instance:

<table>
    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
        <td>14</td>
    </tr>
</table>

John     15
Sarah    14

items.title: <td>: Table Data Cell
items.text:
<td> is a data cell, td = table data:

<td>John</td>

A row can hold several:

<tr>
    <td>John</td>
    <td>15</td>
    <td>S2</td>
</tr>

→ three cells: | John | 15 | S2 |

items.title: <th>: Table Header Cell
items.text:
<th> is a header cell, th = table header. Use it for row or column headings instead of plain <td>:

Instead of:

<tr>
    <td>Name</td>
    <td>Age</td>
    <td>Class</td>
</tr>

prefer:

<tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Age</th>
    <th>Class</th>
</tr>

Full example:

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Class</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
        <td>14</td>
        <td>S1</td>
    </tr>
</table>

That first row now properly labels the columns.

items.title: <caption>: Table Title
items.text:
<caption> gives the table a title or description and belongs right after <table>:

<table>
    <caption>Student Information</caption>

    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Class</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

Think of it as the table's heading, readers and screen readers thank you for it.

items.title: <thead>: Header Group
items.text:
<thead> groups the header rows:

<table>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Name</th>
            <th>Age</th>
            <th>Class</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

</table>

Particularly useful when tables get longer or you want to style the header separately.

items.title: <tbody>: Body Group
items.text:
<tbody> wraps the main data rows:

<table>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Name</th>
            <th>Age</th>
            <th>Class</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>John</td>
            <td>15</td>
            <td>S2</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Sarah</td>
            <td>14</td>
            <td>S1</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

</table>

items.title: <tfoot>: Footer / Summary
items.text:
<tfoot> groups summary or footer rows, e.g. a total:

<table>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Product</th>
            <th>Price</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Bread</td>
            <td>5,000</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Milk</td>
            <td>3,000</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <th>Total</th>
            <th>8,000</th>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>

</table>

items.title: Complete Table Structure
items.text:
Putting it together, a well-structured table often looks like:

<table>
    <caption>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>
            <th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>
            <td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <td>
            <td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>

</table>

Concrete example:

<table>

    <caption>Student Marks</caption>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Name</th>
            <th>Mathematics</th>
            <th>English</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>John</td>
            <td>85</td>
            <td>78</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Sarah</td>
            <td>92</td>
            <td>88</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

</table>

items.title: Rows vs Columns: A Quick Visual
items.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Class</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>15</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

→ 2 rows, 3 columns:

             Columns
          ↓       ↓       ↓

       | Name | Age | Class |
       |------|-----|-------|
Rows → | John | 15  | S2    |

Remember: <tr> makes a row; <th>/<td> make cells inside that row.

items.title: Spanning Cells
items.text: Sometimes a cell should stretch over several rows or columns.

items.title: colspan: span columns
items.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <th colspan="2">Student Information</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>S2</td>
    </tr>
</table>

That header now covers two columns.

items.title: rowspan: span rows
items.text:
<table>
    <tr>
        <th rowspan="2">Name</th>
        <td>John</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Sarah</td>
    </tr>
</table>

"Name" stretches over two rows.

items.title: Tables Are for Data, Not Layout
items.text:
Good fits:

Student | Class | Mark
Product | Price | Quantity
Date    | Event | Location

If you're reaching for a table just to position things on the page, pause, layout is a job for CSS (and landmarks like header/main), not tables.

items.title: At a glance
items.text: Element / Attribute What it does <table> Creates a table <caption> Title / description for the table <tr> Table row <th> Header cell <td> Data cell <thead> Groups header rows <tbody> Groups main rows <tfoot> Groups footer / summary rows colspan Span multiple columns rowspan Span multiple rows

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Minimal table:

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Heading</th>
        <th>Heading</th>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>Data</td>
        <td>Data</td>
    </tr>
</table>

More structured:

<table>

    <caption>Table Title</caption>

    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Heading</th>
            <th>Heading</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Data</td>
            <td>Data</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>

    <tfoot>
        <tr>
            <td>Summary</td>
            <td>Total</td>
        </tr>
    </tfoot>

</table>

Keep this in mind:

<table> → <tr> → <th> / <td>

A table holds rows; each row holds cells.

items.title: Forms Basics
items.text: Forms are how users give you information, log in, register, search, give feedback, place an order. If a page needs input, you'll likely need a form.

items.title: What is a Form?
items.text:
It's simply a section of a page where people can enter or pick information. You'll see them for logins, registrations, contact pages, search boxes, surveys and bookings.

A tiny example:

<form>
    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name">

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

items.title: <form>: The Container
items.text:
<form> wraps the controls that collect information:

<form>

    <!-- Form controls go here -->

</form>

Inside you can place things like <input>, <label>, <textarea>, <select>, <button>, <fieldset> and friends.

items.title: <label>: Describing a Control
items.text:
<label> tells users what a field is for. Link it to the input via for ↔ id:

<label for="name">Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name">

for="name"
     ↓
id="name"

That connection also means clicking the label focuses the input, a small usability win.

items.title: <input>: The Workhorse
items.text:
<input> can collect many kinds of data. The type attribute says which:

<input type="text">

Common types:

Type When you'd use it text General text email Email address (browser can validate) password Password (hidden as you type) number Numeric value date Pick a date time Pick a time checkbox Multiple choices radio One choice from a group file File upload search Search box submit Submit the form

items.title: Text Input
items.text:
<label for="name">Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name">

A user might type:

Jonathan

items.title: Email Input
items.text:
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email">

Browsers can then validate the shape of an email and show a suitable keyboard on mobile.

items.title: Password Input
items.text:
<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="password">

Characters are hidden as you type, as you'd expect.

items.title: Number Input
items.text:
<label for="age">Age:</label>
<input type="number" id="age">

You can bound it:

<input type="number" id="age" min="10" max="100">

items.title: Date Input
items.text:
<label for="birthday">Date of Birth:</label>
<input type="date" id="birthday">

The browser will often show a date picker.

items.title: Time Input
items.text:
<label for="appointment">Appointment Time:</label>
<input type="time" id="appointment">

items.title: Textarea: For Longer Text
items.text:
When you need multiple lines, use <textarea>, unlike <input>, it has an opening and closing tag:

<label for="message">Message:</label>

<textarea id="message"></textarea>

Size it with rows/cols if you like:

<textarea id="message" rows="5" cols="40"></textarea>

items.title: Select and Option: Drop-Down
items.text:
<select> creates the list; <option>s are the choices:

<label for="country">Country:</label>

<select id="country">
    <option>Uganda</option>
    <option>Kenya</option>
    <option>Tanzania</option>
    <option>Rwanda</option>
</select>

items.title: Radio Buttons: Pick One
items.text:
Radios let you choose one option from a group. The key is they share the same name:

<p>Gender:</p>

<input type="radio" id="male" name="gender" value="male">
<label for="male">Male</label>

<input type="radio" id="female" name="gender" value="female">
<label for="female">Female</label>


name="gender"
→ tells the browser they belong together.

items.title: Checkboxes: Pick Many
items.text:
Unlike radios, you can tick several boxes:

<p>Languages you know:</p>

<input type="checkbox" id="python" name="language" value="python">
<label for="python">Python</label>

<input type="checkbox" id="javascript" name="language" value="javascript">
<label for="javascript">JavaScript</label>

<input type="checkbox" id="java" name="language" value="java">
<label for="java">Java</label>

items.title: The name Attribute
items.text:
name is what the form sends to the server:

<input type="text" name="username">

Example with both:

<label for="username">Username:</label>
<input type="text" id="username" name="username">
  • id: identifies the element in the page (for <label>).
  • name: identifies the field when submitted.

items.title: The value Attribute
items.text:
value is what gets submitted for that control:

<input
    type="radio"
    id="uganda"
    name="country"
    value="uganda"
>
<label for="uganda">Uganda</label>

If this is selected, the submitted value is uganda.

items.title: Required Fields
items.text:
Add required when a field must be filled before submission:

<label for="email">Email:</label>

<input
    type="email"
    id="email"
    name="email"
    required
>

The browser will block submission until it's done.

items.title: Placeholder Text
items.text:
placeholder shows a temporary hint inside the input:

<input
    type="text"
    id="username"
    name="username"
    placeholder="Enter your username"
>

It fades when you start typing. It should not replace a proper <label>, labels are always needed.

items.title: The Submit Button
items.text:
You need a way to send the form:

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

That type="submit" is the signal to the browser: "submit this form."

items.title: The <button> Element
items.text:
<button>Click Me</button>

Inside forms, be explicit:

<button type="submit">Submit</button>

For a button that doesn't submit (e.g. JS actions):

<button type="button">Click Me</button>

items.title: Form Submission: action and method
items.text:
action says where the data goes:

<form action="/register">
    ...
</form>

method says how:

<form action="/register" method="post">
    ...
</form>

<form action="/search" method="get">
    ...
</form>
  • GET: requesting/searching; values may appear in the URL. Good for searches.
  • POST: creating/changing data; values go in the request body. Good for registrations, logins.

items.title: Complete Example
items.text:
<form action="/register" method="post">

    <h2>Create an Account</h2>

    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input
        type="text"
        id="name"
        name="name"
        required
    >

    <br>

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input
        type="email"
        id="email"
        name="email"
        required
    >

    <br>

    <label for="password">Password:</label>
    <input
        type="password"
        id="password"
        name="password"
        required
    >

    <br>

    <label for="country">Country:</label>

    <select id="country" name="country">
        <option value="uganda">Uganda</option>
        <option value="kenya">Kenya</option>
        <option value="tanzania">Tanzania</option>
    </select>

    <br>

    <label for="message">About You:</label>

    <textarea
        id="message"
        name="message"
        rows="5"
        cols="40"
    ></textarea>

    <br>

    <button type="submit">Register</button>

</form>

items.title: Grouping Controls: <fieldset> and <legend>
items.text:
For larger forms, group related fields:

<fieldset>

    <legend>Personal Information</legend>

    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

    <label for="email">Email:</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

</fieldset>

<fieldset> is the group; <legend> is its title.

items.title: At a glance
items.text: Element / Attribute What it does <form> Wraps the form <label> Describes a form control <input> Creates an input <textarea> Multi-line text input <select> Drop-down list <option> An option in the list <button> Clickable button <fieldset> Groups related controls <legend> Title for a fieldset type Kind of input or button id Identity in the page name Name sent on submission value Value submitted required Must be completed placeholder Temporary hint action Where data is sent method How data is sent

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Core shape:

<form>

    <label for="name">Name:</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>

</form>

Structure within:

<form>
    ├── <label>
    ├── <input>
    ├── <textarea>
    ├── <select>
    │     └── <option>
    └── <button>
</form>

Forms give you the structure for collecting information. HTML defines the fields and what they mean; the server then receives and does something with that data.

items.title: Grouping: div, section, span
items.text: As pages get bigger, you'll need ways to bundle related bits together. <div>, <section> and <span> all group content, but they signal different things.

items.title: Why group at all?
items.text:
Imagine a page outline:

Header
    Navigation

Main content
    About us
    Our services

Footer

Without grouping, everything's just floating. HTML gives you distinct elements for those bundles.

items.title: <div>: Generic Block Container
items.text:
<div> is your generic block wrapper, it groups content without saying what it means:

<div>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We build software for businesses.</p>
</div>

It simply says:

These elements belong together.

That's why <div> is handy when no more specific semantic element fits.

items.title: <div> as a Container
items.text:
A <div> can hold pretty much anything:

<div>
    <h2>Student Information</h2>

    <p>Name: Jonathan</p>
    <p>Class: S2</p>

    <a href="profile.html">View Profile</a>
</div>

It keeps that cluster together and gives CSS or JavaScript a convenient hook to target.

items.title: <section>: A Thematic Section
items.text:
<section> is for a thematically related chunk of the document, a section with its own topic:

<section>
    <h2>About Us</h2>

    <p>
        We teach students how to build websites.
    </p>
</section>

Unlike <div>, it carries meaning:

This is a distinct section of the document.

items.title: Sections Usually Have a Heading
items.text:
A heading that labels the section helps readers and assistive tech:

<section>
    <h2>Our Services</h2>

    <p>We provide web development services.</p>
</section>

Followed by another:

<section>
    <h2>Contact Us</h2>

    <p>Get in touch with our team.</p>
</section>

Those headings are part of the structure, not just decoration.

items.title: <div> vs <section>: Which One?
items.text:
<div>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We teach programming.</p>
</div>

vs.

<section>
    <h2>About Us</h2>
    <p>We teach programming.</p>
</section>

Both will group, but they say different things:

  • <div> → "Grouped together." No semantics attached.
  • <section> → "This is a meaningful section."

If the bundle represents a real topic-based section, prefer <section>. If you just need a generic box for styling or scripting and nothing semantic fits, use <div>.

items.title: <span>: Generic Inline Container
items.text:
<span> is the inline cousin, it wraps small pieces inside a line:

<p>
    My favourite language is
    <span>Python</span>.
</p>

Unlike <div>, it doesn't start a new block, it stays in the flow of text.

<p>Hello <span>Jonathan</span>, welcome!</p>

That <span> is part of the same paragraph, not a separate block.

items.title: <span> for Part of a Sentence
items.text:
You'll often want to flag a particular phrase:

<p>
    The weather today is
    <span>very warm</span>.
</p>

By itself <span> doesn't add meaning, it just identifies that slice so you can style or script it.

items.title: <span> vs <div>: Inline vs Block
items.text:
<div>: block-level:

<div>
    First group
</div>

<div>
    Second group
</div>
→ each group sits on its own line/ block.

<span>: inline:

<p>
    This is <span>one</span> sentence.
</p>
→ stays within the surrounding line.

Think: block vs inline is the core split.

items.title: Grouping with Classes and IDs
items.text:
These grouping elements get most useful with class or id:

<div class="card">
    <h2>Python</h2>
    <p>A programming language.</p>
</div>

A class marks a category, several elements can share it:

<section class="course">
    <h2>Python Course</h2>
</section>

<section class="course">
    <h2>HTML Course</h2>
</section>

An id identifies one unique element:

<div id="main-content">
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
</div>

You'll lean on them heavily once you add CSS and JavaScript.

items.title: Bringing Them Together
items.text:
A page can use all three at once:

<section>

    <h2>Our Courses</h2>

    <div class="course">
        <h3>HTML</h3>
        <p>Learn how to build <span>web pages</span>.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="course">
        <h3>Python</h3>
        <p>Learn how to build <span>programs</span>.</p>
    </div>

</section>
  • <section> → the Courses section as a whole.
  • <div> → each individual course card.
  • <span> → a small inline highlight inside the paragraph.

items.title: How to Choose
items.text:
Ask what the grouping means:

  • A distinct thematic section? → <section>: 

    <section>
    <h2>Our Services</h2>
    ...
</section>

  • Just need a generic block box? → <div>: 

    <div>
    ...
</div>

  • A small inline slice? → <span>: 

    <p>This is <span>important</span> information.</p>

items.title: At a glance
items.text: Element What it's for <section> Groups thematically related content <div> Generic block-level container <span> Generic inline container class Marks elements as belonging to a group id Unique identifier for one element

items.title: Recap
items.text:
In short:

<section>
    A meaningful section of the document
</section>

<div>
    A generic block-level group
</div>

<p>
    Some text with a
    <span>small inline group</span>
    inside it.
</p>

Mental shorthand:

<section> = meaningful group

<div> = generic block

<span> = generic inline

items.title: Page Landmarks: header, nav, main, footer, article, aside
items.text: Instead of wrapping everything in <div>, HTML gives us elements that say what each part of the page is for. That helps browsers, search engines and screen readers, and it makes your code much easier to follow.

items.title: A typical page structure
items.text:
A straightforward page might look like this:

<body>

    <header>
        <h1>My Website</h1>
    </header>

    <nav>
        <a href="index.html">Home</a>
        <a href="about.html">About</a>
        <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
    </nav>

    <main>

        <article>
            <h2>Learning HTML</h2>
            <p>HTML is used to structure web pages.</p>
        </article>

        <aside>
            <h2>Related Topics</h2>
            <p>Learn about CSS and JavaScript next.</p>
        </aside>

    </main>

    <footer>
        <p>Copyright 2026 My Website</p>
    </footer>

</body>

The takeaway: each element tells us the purpose of its content, not just how it should look.

items.title: <header>: Introductory content
items.text:
Think of <header> as the intro for a page or a section:

<header>
    <h1>My Website</h1>
    <p>Learn web development</p>
</header>

A site header often holds a logo, site name, heading, or a bit of intro text. For example:

<header>
    <h1>Uganda Travel Guide</h1>
    <p>Discover places to visit in Uganda.</p>
</header>

items.title: It doesn't have to be at the very top
items.text:
<header> can also live inside another element:

<article>

    <header>
        <h2>10 Places to Visit in Uganda</h2>
        <p>Published on October 1, 2026</p>
    </header>

    <p>Uganda has many interesting places to visit...</p>

</article>

Here the header belongs to the <article>, not the whole page.

items.title: <nav>: Important navigation
items.text:
<nav> wraps major navigation links:

<nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="about.html">About</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

Use it for main site nav, section nav, or a table of contents, e.g.:

<nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="courses.html">Courses</a>
    <a href="projects.html">Projects</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

items.title: Not every link needs <nav>
items.text:
Inline links like this are fine without it:

<p>
    Read our <a href="privacy.html">privacy policy</a>.
</p>

Save <nav> for genuinely important navigation blocks.

items.title: <main>: The primary content
items.text:
<main> holds the core content of that page:

<main>
    <h1>Learning HTML</h1>

    <p>
